q-113517:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (9-5x)^{-3}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=9-5x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (9-5x)^{-3}\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{-3}\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\int {u}^{-3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}){u}^{-2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{10{u}^{2}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{10(9-5x)^{2}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{10(9-5x)^{2}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{1}{10(9-5x)^{2}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(9-5x)^{-2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\cdot (-2)(9-5x)^{-3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9-5x)+0 \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}(9-5x)^{-3}\cdot (-5) \\  & =(9-5x)^{-3} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(9-5x)}^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-12498:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (5x+1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we let $u=5x+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5x+1)^{1/2}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{1/2}\cdot (\frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}(5x+1)^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{2}{15}\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}+C] & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\sqrt{(5x+1)^{3}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(5x+1)^{3/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{2}{15}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(5x+1)^{1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x+1)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(5x+1)^{1/2}\cdot 5 \\  & =(5x+1)^{1/2} \\  & =\sqrt{5x+1}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-49439:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (x-100)^{7/4}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Now, we let  $u=x-100.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $u$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x-100)^{7/4}\,\text{d}x & =\int {u}^{7/4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{11/4}}{11/4}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{11}(x-100)^{11/4}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{11}\sqrt[4]{(x-100)^{11}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\frac{4}{11}\sqrt[4]{(x-100)^{11}}+C] & =\frac{4}{11}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[\sqrt[4]{(x-100)^{11}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{4}{11}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(x-100)^{11/4}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =\frac{4}{11}\cdot \frac{11}{4}(x-100)^{7/4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x-100)+0 \\  & =(x-100)^{7/4}\cdot 1 \\  & =\sqrt[4]{(x-100)^{7}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-43308:
First, use the identity $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ) & =(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }) \\  & =(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }) \\  & =\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we expand the parentheses in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the numerator using $1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-65218:
First, we expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x(\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the identity $\operatorname{csc}⁡x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ to further simplify the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{2\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}-\frac{2\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}} \\  & =2-2{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =2(1-{cos}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡x=1-{cos}^{2}⁡x$ to rewrite the expression on the right-hand side.

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡x(\operatorname{csc}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\cdot {cos}^{2}⁡x)=2{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

q-23526:
Since both fractions are over a common denominator, we can add them. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{1-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $ to simplify the expression in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{1-2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }+\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

q-1583:
First, we use the definition of $\operatorname{cot}⁡A$ to rewrite the second term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡A}-\frac{1}{{cot}^{2}⁡A} & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡A}-{tan}^{2}⁡A \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡A}-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡A}{{cos}^{2}⁡A} \\  & =\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡A}{{cos}^{2}⁡A}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use the identity $1-{sin}^{2}⁡A={cos}^{2}⁡A$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡A}{{cos}^{2}⁡A} & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡A}{{cos}^{2}⁡A}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡A}-\frac{1}{{cot}^{2}⁡A}=1
$$

q-119864:
First, we rewrite the numerator using $1-{sin}^{2}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x.$

$$
\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1}=\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1}
$$

Next, we factor the numerator as a difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1} & =\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1} \\  & =-\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cancel{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}}{\cancel{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}} \\  & =-\frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1} \\  & =-(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1}=-(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x).
$$

q-65182:
First, we rewrite the denominator using $1-{cos}^{2}⁡x={sin}^{2}⁡x.$

$$
\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}=\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1-{cos}^{2}⁡x}
$$

Next, we factor the denominator as difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1-{cos}^{2}⁡x} & =\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}{\cancel{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$

q-31600:
Note that plugging in $x=-1$ gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)}{{x}^{2}+3x+2} & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{[x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)]^{′}}{[{x}^{2}+3x+2]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+2)+\frac{x}{x+2})}{2x+3} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(-1+2)+\frac{-1}{-1+2})}{2(-1)+3} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-1}{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

q-72333:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡x=-\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}{e}^{1/x}=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{-\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{e}^{1/x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{ln}⁡x]^{′}}{[{e}^{1/x}]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{{e}^{1/x}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{{x}^{-1}}{{e}^{1/x}\cdot {x}^{-2}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{x}{{e}^{1/x}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-72336:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}]}^{′}}{{[\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(-\frac{4}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{-3}}{4{x}^{-5}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-31517:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[x\operatorname{ln}⁡x]^{′}}{[{e}^{x}]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}{{e}^{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1}{{e}^{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1]^{′}}{[{e}^{x}]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{x})}{{e}^{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{x{e}^{x}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49453:
First, let $u=x+4.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{x+4}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-15707:
First, let $u=x+1.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{x+1}\,\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-72446:
First, let $u=5-2x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+C & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-2x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-2x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{5-2x}\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|5-2x|).
$$
